disease_info: Bipolar II Disorder is characterized by a recurrent course of depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, with no history of full manic episodes. Hypomanic periods involve persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy, but without the marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychosis seen in mania. Depressive episodes are often more frequent and disabling, and patients typically present during these lows rather than during hypomania, which may be experienced as productive or ego-syntonic. It is distinguished from unipolar depression by the presence of hypomanic episodes and from Bipolar I Disorder by the absence of full mania, and it commonly emerges in late adolescence or early adulthood with a chronic, episodic course.

narrative.stressor: Nelly’s symptoms became clinically significant during a tax season when her small accounting firm was short‑staffed and she volunteered to take on extra client accounts to prove she was ready to start CPA coursework. For several weeks she rode a wave of unusually intense productivity, staying up late tweaking spreadsheets and sketching plans for a side business offering bookkeeping to local Latino entrepreneurs, while still trying to keep up with salsa classes and weekend hikes. As the rush ended, she abruptly found herself unable to maintain her usual meticulous routines at work; errors began appearing in ledgers, she stopped going to art workshops, and her normally detailed travel and study plans felt overwhelming rather than exciting. Her supervisor’s concern about recent mistakes, combined with her own distress at how uncharacteristically disengaged she felt from both work and the community events she usually loved, led her to seek a mental health evaluation after about a month of noticeable change.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Over the last month I’ve just lost interest in my art, dancing, and even my job, and I can’t seem to care about anything the way I used to.”

narrative.stressor: Rafael’s pattern of mood shifts became problematic after his part‑time maintenance hours were cut when the office building where he worked lost several tenants, tightening his already fragile budget. In response, he went through a brief stretch of feeling unusually driven and confident, sketching out elaborate plans to take on more side repair jobs and even talking about starting a small independent handyman service, only to abandon most of these ideas as his energy and motivation dropped off. Over the following weeks he struggled to keep up with the few remaining shifts, fell behind on rent, and started skipping his usual calming routines like lakefront walks and model building, spending more time alone in his apartment worrying about money. When a cousin noticed the unpaid bills piling up and how unlike himself he seemed, she pushed him to go to a community clinic, where he agreed to talk to a psychiatrist after admitting that the financial stress felt unbearable and he couldn’t think clearly enough to sort it out.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My head feels foggy and I can’t focus long enough to figure out my bills or make decisions about work anymore.”

narrative.stressor: For Marta, the turning point came during a particularly tense season at home and work, when her teenage daughter was pushing against family rules and her spouse was working longer hours, leaving her feeling caught in the middle. Around the same time, a successful rollout of a new hospitality program at her workplace left her unusually energized and socially outgoing for several weeks, leading her to impulsively add new initiatives and overcommit to community events and art workshops. As that surge of activity tapered off, she found herself increasingly emotionally raw and self‑critical about minor conflicts with staff and family, canceling hikes and yoga classes and having trouble keeping up with schedules she used to manage despite her relaxed style. After a heated argument with her daughter about her inconsistency at home and a colleague gently suggesting she seemed "not like herself" for the past month, Marta consulted her primary care provider, who referred her for psychiatric assessment to understand the pattern behind these fluctuating periods and the strain they were placing on her relationships.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I’ve been overwhelmed by guilt about letting everyone down at home and at work, even when people tell me it’s not that bad.”
